senses: Accompanied by tears; crying, or about to cry.
ety: From tear + -ful.
examples: Aaron got a little tearful until Laura came to reassure him.

The week that was yet to elapse, she spent in wandering through her uncle's favourite walks in hours of tearful vigil, beside his tomb, and in collecting together every trifle on which he had set a value.

senses: Finished; over with; done.
ety: From Italian finito (“finished”), from Latin fīnītus. Doublet of finite.
examples: No more kink. Nothing. Finito. Got it?

senses: One who tilts something.
One who operates a tilt hammer.
ety: From tilt + -er.
examples: I love the way everyone tilts their heads as they scan the shelves. That's how I think of us book readers: we're head tilters.

senses: The act of calling or assembling by summons.
An assembly or meeting.
An academic assembly, in which the business of a university is transacted.
A flock of eagles.
ety: From Middle English convocacioun, from Old French convocation, from Latin convocatio, convocationem.
examples: A convocation of eagles around the four corners of the army field flew in.
A convocation of eagles noticed that the young bird was without his mother and took pity on him.

senses: A (commercial) facility where eggs, especially those of fish or poultry, are hatched under artificial conditions.
A place where something is fostered or nurtured; a nursery.
ety: From hatch (verb) + -ery (suffix denoting a place where an art, craft, or practice is carried out).
examples: The codfish hatchery at Wood's Hole, Massachusetts, has been highly successful.

senses: Of less than a traditional or accepted standard.
ety: From sub- + par.
examples: Bob's grasp of English was subpar.
They and their siblings were the only black kids at their respective Catholic schools in middle America. They were treated as subpar.

senses: To enlarge; to make bigger.
To become wider or larger; to expand.
To speak largely and copiously; to dwell in narration; to enlarge; with "on" or "upon".
examples: The eye doctor put drops in my eye to dilate the pupil so he could see the nerve better.
His heart dilates and glories in his strength.
But still they on their ancient joys dilate.

senses: A Maori house or other building.
A rough shack or hut built (by Europeans) using traditional Maori techniques; a workman's shack.
ety: Borrowed from Māori whare (“house, hut”).
examples: We were on the brow of the hill, and below us there was a whare roofed in with corrugated iron.
At the far end of the whare there's a wooden bed.

senses: A small opening or space between objects, especially adjacent objects or objects set closely together, such as between cords in a rope, components of a multiconductor electrical cable or atoms in a crystal.
A fragment of space.
An interval of time required by the Roman Catholic Church between the attainment of different degrees of an order.
A small interval of time free to be spent on activities other than one's primary goal.
ety: From late Middle English interstice, from Old French interstice or directly from Latin interstitium (“a space between, gap, interval”), ultimately from intersistere (“to stand in between, to stop in the middle”), from inter- + sistere (“to stand, to stop”).
examples: Relics of the British empire now mostly survive in the interstices of the global economy. They are the major winners from the fiscal haemorrhage that has resulted from financial globalisation.

senses: A telegrapher or telegraph operator.
ety: From telegraph + -ist.
examples: But the next stations, Wamphray, and Dinwoodie, were small places, very probably with no night telegraphists.

senses: Characteristic of, or in the manner of, an adversary; combative, hostile, opposed.
ety: Probably from adversary + -al
examples: The White Paper therefore aims to tackle complexity rather then ownership of the railways, and to eliminate "the adversarial relationships between operators, suppliers, NR and government".

senses: One-twentieth of a ream of paper; a collection of twenty-four or twenty-five sheets of paper of the same size and quality, unfolded or having a single fold.

A set of leaves which are stitched together, originally a set of four pieces of paper (eight leaves, sixteen pages). This is most often a single signature (i.e. group of four), but may be several nested signatures.
A book, poem, or pamphlet.
ety: From Middle English quayer, from Anglo-Norman quaier and Old French quaer, from Latin quaternus (“fourfold”), from quater (“four times”). Doublet of cahier.
examples: Under the year 1533 we are told that the ream contained twenty quires.

senses: Hammered or pressed in (usually on a coin).
ety: From Latin incūsus, past participle of incūdō, from in- + cūdō.
examples: The back of the coin bears an incuse coat of arms.

senses: One who provides a rating or assessment.
ety: From rate (“to appraise”) + -er.
examples: The three raters agreed on the score.

senses: Cautious, suspicious, wary, hesitant, or nervous about something; having reservations or concerns.
Leering; lecherous or unpleasant.
ety: First attested in 1718, “untrustful, suspicious”, either from leer (“sideward look”) + -y, lear (“learning, knowledge”) + -y. More at leer, lear.
examples: Since he was bitten by a dog when he was young, he has always been leery of animals.
It probably seems crazy, crazy, a graveyard theory A ghost tried to approach me, he got leery
And there was a particularly brutal villain with leery eyes, ugly mouth, with one tooth gone, and an iron jaw like a hull-dog's.

senses: One of a group of vitamins that act against the effects of free radicals.
ety: From anti- + oxidant.
examples: The postulated mechanism for the reaction of coumarin 4 as an antioxidant, as indicated in Fig 3, relies on the mercapto hydrogen atom (bold), which is under the influence of resonance and inductive effects.

senses: An offshoot of a decision, fact etc.; a consequence or implication, especially one which complicates a situation.
ety: From Middle French ramification, or its source, Medieval Latin rāmificātiō. By surface analysis, ramify + -ication.
examples: What, then, is my Scheme? It is a very simple one, although in its ramifications and extensions it embraces the whole world.
He stirred up a bigger muss than he had anticipated, and even he was astounded at the wide ramifications of the struggle and at the unexpected and incongruous interests that were drawn into it.

But most often and memorably his work falls into that territory best summed up as speculative fiction, with a particular emphasis on dystopian futures and the existential ramifications of space exploration.

senses: An animal, especially a calf, born prematurely or abortively.
ety: From an allusive sense of slink (“to bring forth young prematurely”).
examples: Then I met a great guy, Placenta Juan the Afterbirth Tycoon. Made his in slunks during the war. (Slunks are underage calves trailing afterbirths and bacteria, generally in an unsanitary and unfit condition.)

Calf heads were tanned from yearling calves less than a year in age. Slunk skins were tanned from unborn calfskins which, gruesome as it sounds, were often by products of the cow slaughtering process.

senses: Thin, pliable, and often transparent.
ety: From Middle French membraneux; equivalent to membrane + -ous.
examples: The microcannon starts with a membranous polymer film.

senses: A tall, cylindrical Eastern European Easter bread, traditional in the Orthodox Christian faith.
ety: From Russian кулич (kulič), ultimately from Ancient Greek κόλλιξ (kóllix, “roll or loaf of bread”). Cognate to Persian کلوچه، کلیچه (koluče, količe). Doublet of kulcha.
examples: One of the most famous of all Easter breads is the Russian kulich, a tall but delicate sweet yeasted bread that is sugared and decorated with the initials XB, which stand for “Christ is risen.”

senses: The Anglo-Saxon national council or witenagemot.
ety: Learned borrowing from Old English witan, plural of wita (“wise man”).
examples: But in estimating the powers of the witan, we must not lose sight of the fact, that the king sometimes assumes a tone of superiority scarcely consistent with its independence.
The folkland, the national fund, was administered and conveyed conjointly by the king and the witan.

senses: The act of deflagrating; an intense fire; a conflagration or explosion. Specifically, combustion that spreads subsonically via thermal conduction.
ety: From Latin dēflagrātiō, from dēflagrāre.
examples: If, for example, the mixture of oxygen and hydrogen was twenty volumes, and three volumes of oxygen remained after the deflagration, the mixture consisted of six volumes of hydrogen and six volumes of oxygen.
Black powder . . . It produces a relatively fast burn or deflagration rather than a detonation and is classified as "low explosive".

senses: The vault of the heavens, where the clouds, sun, moon, and stars can be seen; the heavens, the sky.
The field or sphere of an activity or interest.
The abode of God and the angels; heaven.
ety: From Middle English firmament, furmament (“heaven; sky”), from Old French firmament (“firmament”), or from its etymon Latin firmāmentum (“support; sky”), from firmāre (“to strengthen”) + -mentum (suffix indicating an instrument or medium, or the result of an action). Firmāre is the present active infinitive of firmō (“to make firm, strengthen”), from firmus (“firm, strong, stable”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold; to support”). The Latin word was used in the Vulgate version of the Bible to translate the Ancient Greek στερέωμα (steréōma, “foundation, framework; firmament”)
examples: And far above the gentle moon sails on / Through the blue firmament. It is a scene / That gives that spot of earth the air of Heav'n!
On its far side, on the very horizon of the world, stood purple mountains, so tall and sharp that they bridged the firmaments.

By this time, Seaford was a town of 2,000 people, and, in the next decade, the poultry industry became a rising star in the firmament of economic growth as new housing and feeding techniques were introduced.

senses: Offensive or repulsive; arousing disgust or aversion.
ety: From Middle English repugnaunt, from Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare (“to oppose, to fight against”), from re- (“back, against”) + pugnare (“to fight”); see pugnacious. By surface analysis, re- + Latin pugn + -ant.
examples: Repugnant is a creature who would squander the ability to lift an eye to heaven conscious of his fleeting time here

senses: An assistant to someone who holds a position in the military or civil service.
An assistant mayor of a French commune.
ety: From French adjoindre (“to join”), from late 19th C; see also adjoin. Doublet of adjunct. In the case of category theory (which brings together concepts from numerous fields), the term is often confounded with adjunct and the relationship is called an adjunction. The origin of any particular usage may therefore be uncertain.
examples: The chef and his adjoints are seen by this code as part of the military, subject to military jurisdiction despite their obligation to execute the orders of the administrative council and of the justice of the peace.
A vigorous, aggressive, and ambitious mayor will not rely overmuch upon his adjoints, but a mayor of the more passive type will lean heavily upon them.
Mayors and their adjoints were often simple cultivateurs like the majority of the community.

senses: Spacious, expansive, comfortable.
ety: From room + -y.
examples: Our new apartment is roomy enough to accommodate all our furniture.
The cab, with two side windows, was one of the most roomy and comfortable in the country at that time.

So BMW has conjured a tweener — a roomier hatchback on platform shoes, with standard all-wheel drive — to attract customers who crave the 3 Series’ performance but need more utility to close the deal.

senses: An inexpensive waterproof covering used especially for floors, made from solidified linseed oil over a burlap or canvas backing, or from its modern replacement, polyvinyl chloride.
ety: From Latin līnum (“flax”) + oleum (“oil”). Coined by English manufacturer and inventor Frederick Walton c. 1864 and used as a trade name but never registered as a trademark. It was the first product whose name was ruled to be genericized.
examples: The house seemed unfamiliar in the dark stormy light; the red and purple glass of the front door made livid bruises on the linoleum; the green chenille curtain was like a veil of seaweed.

senses: Countenance; one's face.
The appearance or aspect of something, especially when expressive or distinctive.
ety: From Middle English visage, from Anglo-Norman visage, from Vulgar Latin *vīsāticum, derived from Latin vīsus (“appearance, sight”), derived from vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision. See -age (“noun suffix”).
examples: Lying on the floor was a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He was withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage. It was not till they had examined the rings that they recognized who it was.
Snowflakes fell gently across the mountain’s rugged visage.

senses: Containing custard.
Resembling or characteristic of custard in taste, texture, etc.
ety: From custard + -y.
examples: So next morning, once he had started the Dirty Train on its circuit, he made a note, as he went along, of the cage numbers of six of the bluest of the blue bucks and six of the custardiest of the cream does.
Or pop one in a pudding or pie filling mix for a silkier, custardier rendition.

senses: A display, particularly one that presents numerical data.
The information, usually a measurement, shown on such a display.
An account of the topics discussed in a meeting, especially in diplomatic or political contexts.
ety: Deverbal from read out.
examples: Her company retrofitted its manual machine tools with digital readouts.
The density is measured by the readout from a hydrometer.
Most of us first found out when we heard the readout from the summit meeting.

senses: A female tiger; a she-tiger.
ety: From French tigresse, corresponding to tiger + -ess.
examples: So-al was a mighty fine-looking girl, built like a tigress as to strength and sinuosity, but withal sweet and womanly.
Indestructibly seductive at 79, this greatest and wittiest of all singing tigresses has lasted even longer on the stage than the original glamorous grandmother, Marlene Dietrich.

senses: The sphere of human reason, thought, and consciousness, seen as a theoretical evolutionary stage.
ety: Borrowed from French noosphère, from Ancient Greek νόος (nóos, “mind, spirit”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), developed and perhaps coined by Pierre Teilhard de Chardin and Vladimir Vernadsky, in analogy to atmosphere, biosphere etc. By surface analysis, nous (“mind”) + -sphere.
examples: This creates a pattern of homesteading in the noosphere that rather resembles that of settlers spreading into a physical frontier—not random, but like a diffusion-limited fractal.
The noosphere admits human cognition as a part of the environment of the Earth.

senses: Action that works to prevent some bad outcome.
A move or strategy that frustrates an opponent's plan or tactic.
ety: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”) + φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “a watching, guarding”).
examples: The central bankers viewed these moves as prophylaxis against inflation.

senses: A brilliant yellow color, like that of a daffodil.
ety: Variant of Middle English affodill (“ramson”), from Medieval Latin affodillus, from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos), of Pre-Greek origin. The initial d- is perhaps from merging of the article in Dutch de affodil, the Netherlands being a source for bulbs (compare adder, apron, newt, nickname, orange and umpire for this rebracketing process). Doublet of asphodel.
examples: Where ships of purple gently toss / On seas of daffodil, / Fantastic sailors mingle, / And then—the wharf is still.

senses: An underground layer of water-bearing porous stone, earth, or gravel.
ety: From aqui- + -fer.
examples: The water in the well came from an aquifer.

senses: A large grey European goose, Anser anser, with pink legs and dull orange beak.
ety: From grey (“colour”) + lag (“old name for a goose, derived from the call used to move such animals along”).
examples: Greylags used to concentrate on British estuaries, eating roots of rushes and sedges, as they do in other parts of their range.
Earlier, 250 more had flown to Rattray beach, nearly all pinkfeet although I saw four greylags and heard others.

senses: A type of Jewish pastry, which may be filled with various fruit, nuts, chocolate, etc.
ety: From Yiddish ראָגאַל (rogal) with plural suffix ־לעך (-lekh), from Polish rogal (“crescent roll”).
examples: Then he ambles to his dressing room, where rugelach and carrot sticks sit on a coffee table for a postshow nosh.
And while you’re there, you can pick up a babka, which you’ve heard about (a twisted, sweet chocolate loaf) and a bag of rugelach which you might not have (crescent-shaped chocolate pastries).

Rugelach is thought to have the same origin—this staple of Ashkenazi Jewish baking spread across the world and became popular, especially in the US, but not quite to the extent of its French half-brother.

senses: The portion of water in a sample of soil that is not available to vegetation.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”) + ἄρδω (árdō, “to water, to irrigate”).
examples: Grasses sprout on the sands long before the early rains have restored the echard of adjoining clays and given a surplus as chresard which can initiate grass growth.

senses: A generic snack product consisting of an oblong yellow cake with a creamy white filling.
An actor, actress, or public figure regarded primarily for their physical attractiveness rather than for substantive talent, achievement or contribution.
ety: Genericized trademark of Twinkie.
examples: This twinkie was enveloped in an oversize parka with the hood pulled so far forward that all that could be seen of his face was a frostbitten nose and a microphone.
Tom Ford, who said he was “a twinkie” at Studio 54 in the days when Halston hung out there with Liza Minnelli, Liz Taylor, Bianca Jagger and Warhol, was also impressed with Mr. McGregor and the show.

senses: To astonish or stun, especially as a result of some distressing action.
ety: From Middle French stupéfier, from Latin stupefaciō (“strike dumb, stun with amazement, stupefy”), from stupeō (“to be stunned, speechless”) (see English stupid, stupor) + faciō (“to do, make”).
examples: The police's negligence and callousness continued to stupefy her.
What if I love you!—This misery / Of your dissatisfaction and misprision / Stupefies me.
He also believed that idealism of any kind was a more or less disguised form of religion, which was invariably used by exploiters to delude and stupefy the masses.
